revolutionary-battles-1775-1776.works: The red/blue diamond legend is short and clear, every battle pop-up puts the date right under the title, and the numbered circles with their plain 'Victor:' lines tell the story from Lexington to Trenton in a way I could defend to a parent. Image credits are in each pop-up.

findings.where: q1-bookmark and q4-circles views; Turning Points circles over Revolutionary War Battles (and Key Port Cities anchors); Q1 step 4 (Boston diamond) and Q4 steps 2-4 (Fort Washington, Fort Lee, Trenton)
findings.what: In the Massachusetts bookmark I can't see a diamond to click at Boston: circle 2 sits right on it, and only a faint pink and blue tint shows through the white circle. Around New York it's the same: circle 5 covers the Trenton diamond, circle 4 covers a red diamond and opens '1 of 5', and the New York port anchor sits on circle 3. The sheet says the winner is shown only by the diamond's color, and under the circles I can't see the color.
findings.why: The winner is deliberately given only by color, so if the color is hidden students guess, or take it from the turning-point pop-up instead. I'd spend the period walking groups through the pop-up arrows.
findings.suggestion: Move the Turning Points circles off the battle points (a little above and to the side, with a short leader line), or draw the diamonds on top of the circles. Add to Q4 step 1: 'Turn off Key Port Cities first.'
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q1-bookmark.png (circle 2 over Boston); --q2-bunkerhill.png (Boston click opens 1 of 3); --q4-circles.png (circle 5 over Trenton, anchor over circle 3); --q4-circle4.png (1 of 5)

findings.where: All views; basemap and Revolutionary War Battles; Q1 step 5 (Measure Boston to Concord), Q3 steps 3-5 (name the major ports, Measure New York to Philadelphia and to Boston), Q4 step 5 (Measure New York City to Trenton)
findings.what: The map has no town names at all: no Boston, Concord, New York, Philadelphia, Norfolk or Trenton, only colony names and rivers. The diamonds aren't labeled either. Every Measure question assumes students already know where these towns are.
findings.why: Students will measure from the wrong diamond and get answers outside the accepted ranges, and I can't tell a student who knows the geography from one who guessed. A reviewer would say the lesson can't be done as written.
findings.suggestion: Turn on short labels for Revolutionary War Battles (e.g. 'Trenton') at bookmark scales and labels for Key Port Cities, or use a basemap that shows city names. Failing that, name the exact start and end symbols on the sheet ('from the large anchor at Boston to the Lexington and Concord diamond').

findings.where: q3-port; Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781; Reading the map paragraph and Q3 step 4
findings.what: The sheet says this layer has no pop-ups, so students should name ports from the coastline. When I click an anchor, a pop-up opens with the name: 'Stonington, CT'.
findings.why: The sheet has students guessing names the map would give them, and when the sheet contradicts the map students stop trusting the instructions.
findings.suggestion: Change the sheet and lesson page to 'Click an anchor to read the port's name', and check that the large Major Port City symbols open a name too.

findings.where: q2-colony, q2-colony-ny, q2-all; Thirteen British Colonies; Q2 step 3 (click the colony to read its name)
findings.what: Clicking inside Virginia and inside New York opens nothing. The colony names are printed on the map, so most students will manage, but at the zoomed-out view Rhode Island has no label, and the northernmost diamond is in Quebec, which has no label at all because it isn't one of the colonies.
findings.why: The answer key expects Quebec and Rhode Island. Students will write Massachusetts or New York for those diamonds, or leave Quebec out, and I'd have to explain without help from the map that Quebec was a British province, not one of the thirteen.
findings.suggestion: Turn on the colony pop-up the lesson page describes, or reword step 3 to 'Read the colony names printed on the map', and add a label 'Province of Quebec (British)' north of the colonies.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q2-colony.png and --q2-colony-ny.png (no pop-up opened); --q2-all.png (no Rhode Island or Quebec label)

findings.where: q2-all and q2-colony; Revolutionary War Battles; Q2 step 1 (zoom out until you see every diamond, Quebec to South Carolina)
findings.what: At laptop size with the legend open, Quebec is off the top and the South Carolina diamond is half off the bottom. Closing the legend still doesn't bring Quebec into view.
findings.why: Students will think they've seen every diamond and miss the 1775 battle at Quebec.
findings.suggestion: Add a bookmark 'All battles 1775-1776' set from Quebec City to Charleston.

findings.where: q1-lexington; Revolutionary War Battles pop-up, Lexington and Concord; Q1 steps 2 and 5
findings.what: The pop-up says Governor Gage 'drafted the Coercive Acts'. As I understand it, Parliament passed those acts in 1774 and Gage enforced them in Massachusetts; I'd check that against a standard text before using this. It also puts Concord '20 miles northwest of Boston', while the answer key accepts 15 to 17 miles for the straight-line measure.
findings.why: Students copy pop-up text straight into their answers, and a factual slip about the very first battle is just what a parent or a district reviewer would pick on. The 20-mile figure will make careful students think they measured wrong.
findings.suggestion: Reword to 'Parliament passed the Coercive Acts in 1774, and Gage, as governor, enforced them', with a source. Change '20 miles' to 'about 16 miles in a straight line (about 20 by road)'.
findings.evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q1-lexington.png; pop-up text 'He drafted the Coercive Acts' and '20 miles northwest of Boston'

findings.where: q2-bunkerhill; Revolutionary War Battles pop-up, Bunker Hill; Reading the map and Q2 step 2
findings.what: This pop-up does state the result in words ('The Patriots were defeated... a tactical victory for the British'), though the sheet says pop-ups don't. It also says the fight 'confirmed that any reconciliation between England and the American colonies was no longer possible'.
findings.why: I couldn't defend the reconciliation line: Congress still sent the Olive Branch Petition after Bunker Hill (I'd check the date; I believe July 1775). And 'England' should be Great Britain.
findings.suggestion: Rewrite as 'made reconciliation much harder', cite a source, use 'Great Britain', and change the sheet's 'not the winner in words' to 'usually not'.

findings.where: q4-circle4; Turning Points circle 4 (Fall of New York City); Q4 step 2
findings.what: The Battle Details text slips between tenses ('the British build on their advantage', 'The British take control') and says 3,000 soldiers were captured at Fort Washington.
findings.why: Students quote this text. I'd check the figure; I recall it being closer to 2,800.
findings.suggestion: Put the text in the past tense and give the number as 'about 2,800' if that checks out, with a source.

roads-trails-and-rails-west.works: Each trail's pop-up is titled with its name and gives places and dates, and the railroad pop-up gives one clear year ('Railroad in operation by: 1869') with an honest note about missing names. Clicking right on the Union Pacific line still opened that record. The Indigenous layer uses nations' own names, with the English name in brackets for some, which I can explain to parents.

findings.where: q3-indigenous; Indigenous Territories; Q3 'Whose land?' steps 2-4 and the question 'Was the land the trail crossed empty?'
findings.what: With Indigenous Territories turned on and the map zoomed into Wyoming, the shading stops at hard straight lines. Western Wyoming, where the trails run past Rock Springs, has no shading at all, and neither has the band across Colorado and Kansas below the trails. For long stretches the trail looks as if it crosses empty land.
findings.why: The question asks whether the land was empty, and this view says 'partly, yes', the opposite of the answer key and of the history. On a topic about Native nations, that's the one thing I can't let the map get wrong. I'd hold the lesson until it's checked.
findings.suggestion: Check the live layer at this zoom. The square-edged gaps look like features dropped by tile or record limits: raise the layer's record limit, publish it as vector tiles, or simplify the polygons so the whole patchwork draws at every zoom.

findings.where: q3-indigenous; Indigenous Territories labels; Q3 step 4 and its answer
findings.what: The labels I can read along the trail are 'Tsėhéstȯhe (Cheyenne)', 'Oohenumpa', 'Sicangu' and 'Pa'ka'to'de'uk'ethi (Ponca)'. Only some have an English name. The basemap's city of Cheyenne is labeled inside the territories as well. The answer key lists Lakota, Pawnee, Kaw and Shoshone, and none of those names appear in this view.
findings.why: Students can't connect 'Sicangu' to the Lakota (Brulé) in their textbook, and some will write down the city of Cheyenne as a nation. I'd accept the names, but I'd have to explain each one.
findings.suggestion: Add the English or wider group name to every label, e.g. 'Sicangu (Brulé Lakota)' and 'Oohenumpa (Two Kettle Lakota)', and update the answer key to match the names actually printed.

findings.where: q3-indigenous; Indigenous Territories (no pop-up, not in the legend); Reading the map and Q3
findings.what: Nothing on the map tells students where these territories come from or what period they show. The only clue is 'Native Land Digital' in the small attribution strip at the bottom.
findings.why: If a parent asks 'says who, and when?', the answer should be on the map. As I understand it, Native Land Digital describes its own map as approximate and not an authoritative or legal source; I'd check its exact wording and pass it on.
findings.suggestion: Add a layer description or pop-up: 'Approximate territories from Native Land Digital, a community-made map. Territories overlap and changed over time; they are not tied to one year and are not legal boundaries.'

findings.where: q2-oregon; Trails West; Q2 step 2 (click the Oregon Trail)
findings.what: Clicking the Oregon Trail in Nebraska opened the Pony Express Trail pop-up, 1 of 4. Four trails share the Platte valley there, and their dark dotted colors (Oregon olive, California dark olive, Mormon Pioneer nearly black, Pony Express dark red) look alike on the map and in the legend.
findings.why: Unless students page through to the right record, they'll copy the Pony Express figure (1,800 miles) as the length of the Oregon Trail.
findings.suggestion: Change step 2 to 'Click the Oregon Trail where it runs on its own, in Idaho or Oregon', and make the four colors easier to tell apart (e.g. a brighter yellow-green for Oregon).

findings.where: q4-railroads; Railroads 1826 to 1911 and Transcontinental Railroads completed by 1911; Reading the map and Q4 step 2
findings.what: The 'thin gray lines' show as a dense black mesh at full view, covering the trails in the east. The legend panel cuts off below 'Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific)', so students have to scroll to find Southern Pacific.
findings.why: Students looking for gray lines won't recognize the black mesh, and the trail dots east of Denver disappear under it.
findings.suggestion: Lighten the 1826-1911 lines to a real light gray with some transparency; if they stay dark, change the sheet to 'thin dark lines'.

findings.where: q2-oregon; basemap; Q2 step 3 (find Independence, Missouri, next to Kansas City)
findings.what: At this zoom Kansas City has a label but Independence doesn't. It may appear closer in; I'd check.
findings.why: Students have to start Measure at Independence, and the answer range depends on it.
findings.suggestion: Change step 3 to 'Zoom in on Kansas City until Independence appears', or mark Independence on the map.

us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850.works: The four shades are easy to read, the free-slave line along Pennsylvania's southern border and the Ohio River is plain, and the slave-trade lines visibly come together on the Gulf at New Orleans. State pop-ups use factual, people-first wording ('a state that allowed the enslavement of people') and name the 1920 source with a 'current scholarship may differ' note, which I can point a parent to.

findings.where: q2-line; Missouri Compromise Line over US States and Territories 1850; Q2 steps 1-2
findings.what: Clicking the gray dashed line opened 'Unorganized Territory' with no arrows, so the line's own pop-up (its name, 1820 and the note about Missouri) never appeared.
findings.why: Students can get 1820 by luck from the territory text, but they miss the explanation of why Missouri was the exception, which is the point of the question.
findings.suggestion: Make the line easier to hit (thicker stroke or a wider click tolerance) and draw it above the states so its pop-up comes first. Add to the sheet: 'If a territory opens, click right on the dashes.'
findings.evidence: us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850--q2-line.png; pop-up 'Unorganized Territory ... Free by Missouri Compromise'

findings.where: q1-pennsylvania; US States and Territories 1850 pop-up; Q1 step 3 (read the year each state became free or slave)
findings.what: Pennsylvania's pop-up says the state 'passed legislation against the enslavement of people 1780', and two lines later that the source records it as 'Abolition by state action between 1830-1850'.
findings.why: Students reading for the year get two answers in the same box. Also, Pennsylvania's 1780 law was gradual and people were still enslaved there for decades afterwards (I'd check the census figures), so 'passed legislation against' needs careful wording.
findings.suggestion: Check Pennsylvania against the scan in the US 1850 Original Map layer and correct the classification field. Word it 'passed a gradual abolition law in 1780'.

findings.where: q4-bookmark; Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade; Q3 steps 2-4 (click the states where the lines begin)
findings.what: One solid black slave-trade line runs through southern Indiana and southern Illinois, well inside the brown free-state shading, from Cincinnati past Evansville towards the Mississippi, crossing the orange Underground Railroad routes. It looks meant to follow the Ohio River but sits north of it.
findings.why: Students who click where that line begins could read 'Ohio' or 'Indiana' and write that the slave trade started in a free state. A parent who sees a slave-trade route running through Indiana will ask me about it.
findings.suggestion: Redraw the line along the river (or the Kentucky bank) and add a pop-up: 'River route down the Ohio and Mississippi'.

findings.where: q4-bookmark; Underground Railroad Approximate Routes and Cities; Q4 steps 1-3
findings.what: The bookmark stops at Detroit and Toledo. The legend panel covers eastern Ohio and the Lake Erie ports, and the only Canadian dot I can see is cut off at the panel edge ('Cha...'). Toronto and Montreal aren't in view. Chicago, Detroit and Indianapolis are each labeled twice (orange and basemap gray).
findings.why: The answer is 'into Canada', and the bookmark doesn't show Canada. Students will answer 'to Lake Erie' or 'Chicago'.
findings.suggestion: Set the bookmark, or add a second one called 'Routes to Canada', to take in Lake Erie, southern Ontario and Montreal with the legend panel open.

findings.where: q1-pennsylvania, q2-missouri, q2-line; every US States and Territories 1850 pop-up
findings.what: Every state pop-up says 'It is recorded on the primary source as:', and the footnote then explains that the source is Harper's Atlas of American History, published in 1920.
findings.why: A 1920 atlas is a secondary source for 1850. We teach that difference in 8th grade, and a reviewer would catch it straight away.
findings.suggestion: Change to 'It is recorded on the source map (Harper's Atlas of American History, 1920) as:'.

findings.where: open and q3-slavetrade legends; Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade (Route of L'Amistead, Route of the Creole, Sea Routes); Reading the map
findings.what: The legend spells it 'Route of L'Amistead', while the sheet says Amistad. None of these lines opens a pop-up, so students see two ships' routes with no dates or story. As far as I know the Amistad was a Spanish ship sailing from Cuba (1839), not part of the US internal trade, yet it sits in a layer called 'Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade'.
findings.why: A misspelling and a mislabel on the most sensitive layer of the map is exactly what gets materials pulled after a complaint. The only source for these lines is on the lesson page, not on the map.
findings.suggestion: Correct it to 'Route of the Amistad (1839)'. Give each ship a pop-up with its date, one factual sentence and a source. Rename the layer 'Slave trade routes' or move the Amistad to its own layer, and add a pop-up to the internal routes saying they are traced from Harper's Atlas (1920) and simplified.

findings.where: q1-pennsylvania; US States and Territories 1850; Q1
findings.what: The 1850 layer draws today's West Virginia boundary inside Virginia, and the answer notes say Missouri is drawn twice, in two different slave groups.
findings.why: West Virginia didn't exist until 1863, so students listing slave states will include it, and the answer notes already have to tell me not to mark the counts. That's hard to defend on a map titled 1850.
findings.suggestion: Merge West Virginia into Virginia and remove the second Missouri shape, so the counts in the answer notes can be definite.

findings.where: open and q4-bookmark; Underground Railroad Approximate Routes; Reading the map and Q4
findings.what: The routes are drawn as dense, definite orange lines. Nothing on the map says they're an early-1900s interpretation; only the lesson page mentions it.
findings.why: Historians question how fixed and organized these routes were. I want students to see the caveat where they see the lines, not only hear it from me.
findings.suggestion: Add a pop-up or layer description: 'Approximate routes from an early-1900s interpretation; people escaping slavery took many different paths', and name the source.

findings.where: open and q2-line; US States and Territories 1850 legend and basemap labels; Q1 and Q2
findings.what: The legend text is copied from the 1920 map ('Acts of Congress admitting Texas, Act of 1848...', 'by old French law') and is cut off at the bottom of the panel. Zoomed in, the basemap prints modern names, OKLAHOMA, COLORADO and WYOMING, over the 1850 territories, and the area that was Indian Territory has no name of its own.
findings.why: Students will write 'Oklahoma' as a slave territory, and the nations removed there disappear from the map. Utah and New Mexico shaded as slave 'by compromise' also need explaining: the Compromise of 1850 left slavery there to popular sovereignty. I'd check how the scan shows them.
findings.suggestion: Add one plain-language line under each legend group, turn off the basemap's modern state labels (or use a basemap without them), and label 'Indian Territory' on the layer.

civil-war-battlefields.works: The states legend says plainly what happened ('Union slave state (border state)', 'Slave state seceding before Fort Sumter, April 1861'), which is factual and defensible, and West Virginia is labeled and shaded, so 'which state didn't exist in 1861' works. The white dashed boundary running past Washington is clear.

findings.where: q3-railroads; Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static); Q3 steps 2-3 (compare railroads north and south of the boundary)
findings.what: With the states layer off and the map zoomed to show the boundary from Virginia west to Kentucky and Tennessee, there are no railroad lines anywhere, north or south, just diamonds on the basemap. The lines only appear when I zoom in close, as in the Antietam view around Maryland.
findings.why: Students will answer 'neither side had railroads' or give up. At the zoom this question needs, the map can't answer it.
findings.suggestion: Remove or widen the visible scale range on Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static) so it draws at regional and national views, and add a bookmark for Q3 that shows both sides of the boundary.
findings.evidence: civil-war-battlefields--q3-railroads.png (no railroad lines); --q4-diamond.png (thin dark lines appear only zoomed in)

findings.where: open and q2-dc; Civil War Battlefields over U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863); Reading the map and Q4 step 3
findings.what: Union Victory diamonds are the same slate blue as the Union states, and Confederate Victory diamonds the same dark brown as the seceded states. In Pennsylvania the big Gettysburg diamond is only a shade darker than the state, and brown diamonds in Georgia and Tennessee nearly disappear.
findings.why: The result is shown only by color, so students will misread battles or miss them, especially the small ones.
findings.suggestion: Give battle results colors the states don't use (e.g. distinct hues with a white outline), or lighten the state fills.

findings.where: q4-gettysburg; Civil War Core Areas and Civil War Battlefield Boundary; Q4 step 2 (click the tan areas and read their names)
findings.what: Clicking Gettysburg opened '1 of 2': 'The battlefield area in the Battle of GETTYSBURG during the CIVIL WAR. It spans 14,508 acres.' The highlighted shape is the striped core, not the whole battlefield, and no state is given. The answer notes give 73,551 acres and a two-letter state code. On the blue Union states, the 'tan' areas look pale gray.
findings.why: Students will report different acreages for the same battle with no way to tell which is which, and the state code the answer notes rely on isn't in the pop-up.
findings.suggestion: Title the core pop-up 'Core area (heaviest fighting)' and the other 'Whole battlefield', add the state to both, write the battle name in normal capitals, and update the answer notes to match what the pop-up shows.

findings.where: open and q2-dc; U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) labels; Q1 and Q2 steps 1-2
findings.what: At the opening view Arkansas and Alabama have no labels. At the Washington, D.C. zoom, Maryland has no label while West Virginia, Virginia, Delaware and New Jersey do. Maryland only gets a label when zoomed in further.
findings.why: Q2 asks which two states border the capital, and Arkansas is one of the four states that left after Fort Sumter. The sheet tells students the state names are written on the map.
findings.suggestion: Raise label priority for Maryland, Arkansas and Alabama (or allow labels to overlap), or add a Q2 bookmark at a zoom where Maryland is labeled.

findings.where: open; Civil War Battlefields legend; Reading the map and Q1 step 1
findings.what: The smallest casualty size is labeled '< 0'. The 'U.S. Civil War States and Territories' groups start at the very bottom of the legend panel, below all the battle symbols, so I have to scroll to find the five groups Q1 asks for.
findings.why: 'Fewer than zero casualties' is the kind of error a student or parent points out, and it makes the whole map look careless.
findings.suggestion: Relabel the smallest class (e.g. 'under 1,000'), and either list the states legend first or tell students on the sheet to scroll the legend.

findings.where: q4-diamond; Civil War Battlefields pop-up, Antietam; Q4
findings.what: The Antietam pop-up shows the name twice, a broken picture (just the link text 'American Battlefield Trust') and the dates 'September 16, 1862 – September 18, 1862'.
findings.why: Most textbooks give Antietam as a single day, September 17, 1862, so students will ask which is right. I'd check what the source's three-day range covers.
findings.suggestion: Fix the image link and add a line such as 'Main battle: September 17, 1862'.

the-battle-of-vicksburg.works: The opening view shows the campaign at a glance: the yellow Vicksburg pin, the labeled route pins down the west bank, and the railroad running east through Edwards to Jackson. The battle pop-ups give clear dates (Champion Hill, May 16, 1863; Port Hudson, May 21 – July 9, 1863).

findings.where: q3-battles legend; Civil War Battlefields; Reading the map, Q3 and Q4
findings.what: On this map Confederate Victory is a gray diamond and Inconclusive is yellow. On the Civil War Battlefields map, which uses the same layer name, Confederate is brown and Inconclusive is white. Yellow is also the color of the Vicksburg pin, and the gray Confederate diamond looks like the gray 'Other' circle.
findings.why: My students do these lessons back to back. They'll read gray as 'Other', and may take the yellow pin for an inconclusive battle.
findings.suggestion: Use the same battle symbols as the Civil War Battlefields map, and keep yellow for the Vicksburg pin only.

findings.where: open view; Key Places in the Union March to Vicksburg; Q2 steps 1-2 (which side of the river each pin is on)
findings.what: The label reads 'Miliken's Bend', but the sheet says Milliken's Bend. The pin sits right on the river with its label across the water, so I can't tell which bank it's on.
findings.why: Q2 is about which side of the river each place is on, and the answer key puts Milliken's Bend on the Louisiana side. A misspelled place name on the map is also something a careful reviewer notices.
findings.suggestion: Correct the spelling to Milliken's Bend in the layer, and move the pin onto the west (Louisiana) bank with its label to the west.

findings.where: q1-bookmark and q3-battles; The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark; Q1 step 1 and Q2 step 1
findings.what: The bookmark zooms in so far that Milliken's Bend and Edwards are out of view, and the Bruinsburg Bend label is hidden under the attribution bar at the bottom. The opening view shows all six pins better than the bookmark does.
findings.why: Students open the bookmark and can't find the pins Q2 lists.
findings.suggestion: Set the bookmark to the opening extent: Milliken's Bend down to Bruinsburg Bend and east to Jackson.

findings.where: open, q1-bookmark, q4-porthudson; basemap state names; Q2 step 2 and Q4 steps 4-5
findings.what: Around Vicksburg the basemap shows no Louisiana or Mississippi label. Zoomed out for Port Hudson, only 'Alabama' is labeled; I can't see Louisiana, Arkansas or Texas. The state line along the river is a faint dashed line that wanders away from today's riverbed.
findings.why: Q4 asks students to read the state names west of the river from the basemap, and Q2 needs them to know which side is Louisiana.
findings.suggestion: Add a simple state-name layer (states as of 1863), or a Q4 bookmark at a zoom where the basemap labels Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas.

findings.where: open and q1-bookmark legend; Railroads 1826 to 1911; Q1 steps 3-4
findings.what: The legend lists the Union Pacific, Great Northern, Northern Pacific, Southern Pacific and Central Pacific, none of them anywhere near Mississippi, and the layer includes lines built after the war. In the bookmark view, modern highways (I-20, Highway 80, Highway 61) look a lot like the rail lines.
findings.why: For 'Why Vicksburg?' in 1863 I want only the lines that existed then. The Civil War Battlefields lesson already uses Railroads 1826 to 1863.
findings.suggestion: Use Railroads 1826 to 1863 instead, or filter this layer to lines in operation by 1863, and remove the transcontinental entries from this map's legend.

findings.where: q3-championhill and q4-porthudson; Civil War Battlefields pop-ups; Q3 and Q4
findings.what: Champion Hill and Port Hudson show a broken picture with the link text 'Battlefield Trust page' and 'Tap on image to view page'.
findings.why: That link takes students to an outside website in the middle of the lesson. I need to know what page it opens before I send 8th graders to it, and the broken image looks unfinished.
findings.suggestion: Fix the image, and either name where the link goes ('American Battlefield Trust page on this battle') or remove it.
